checkpoint.prompt_md: About how many probes does binary search need on 1,000,000 sorted elements?
Why write `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2` instead of `(lo + hi) / 2` in Java or C++?
checkpoint.explanation_md: `lo + hi` can exceed the largest 32-bit integer when both are large; `hi - lo` never does.

checkpoint.prompt_md: What does `lower_bound([2, 4, 4, 9], 5)` return — the first index whose value is at least 5?
checkpoint.explanation_md: `a[3] = 9` is the first value ≥ 5, so the answer is index 3 — also where 5 would be inserted.

checkpoint.prompt_md: Binary search only works if the data is ___ (one word).
checkpoint.explanation_md: Discarding half the range is only safe when the order tells you which half cannot contain the target.

modules.title: Sliding Window
modules.summary: Slide fixed windows in O(1) per step; grow and shrink variable windows in one linear pass.

lessons.title: Fixed-size windows
lessons.body_md:
A window is a contiguous stretch `a[l..r]` of an array or string. Many problems ask about every window: the largest sum of k consecutive values, the most distinct letters in any five characters. Recomputing each window from scratch costs O(k) per window; *sliding* it costs O(1).

## Slide, don't recompute

Moving a window of size k one step to the right drops `a[i]` and takes in `a[i + k]`, so its sum updates in constant time:

$$
S_{i+1} = S_i - a_i + a_{i+k}
$$

```python run
def max_window_sum(a, k):
    window = sum(a[:k])            # the first window, summed once
    best = window
    for i in range(k, len(a)):
        window += a[i] - a[i - k]  # take in the new element, drop the old one
        best = max(best, window)
    return best

readings = [3, -1, 4, 1, 5, 9, -2, 6, 5, 3]
print(max_window_sum(readings, 3))  # 15 = 1 + 5 + 9
```

:::callout{kind=complexity time="O(n)" space="O(1)"}
n − k slides of constant work each, instead of (n − k + 1) · k additions.
:::

## A window with a memory: buy low, sell high

"Buy on one day, sell on a later day, maximize the profit" needs only one number from the past: the cheapest price seen so far. Scan once and keep it:

```python run
def max_profit(prices):
    cheapest = float("inf")
    best = 0
    for p in prices:
        cheapest = min(cheapest, p)     # the best day to have bought, so far
        best = max(best, p - cheapest)  # what if we sell today?
    return best

print(max_profit([7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]))  # 5: buy at 1, sell at 6
print(max_profit([7, 6, 4, 3, 1]))     # 0: never sell at a loss
```

:::callout{kind=pitfall title="The day order matters"}
`max(prices) - min(prices)` is wrong: the highest price may come *before* the lowest. The running minimum only ever pairs today's price with an earlier purchase.
:::

:::question{slug=best-time-to-buy-sell-stock}

lessons.title: Growing and shrinking windows
lessons.body_md:
When the window's size is not fixed — "the longest substring with no repeated character", "the shortest stretch that contains every letter of a word" — let it breathe: extend the right edge one step at a time, and whenever the window breaks the rule, shrink it from the left until it is valid again.

## Longest substring without repeats

:::viz{id=sliding-window}

```python run
def longest_unique(s):
    window = set()
    best = l = 0
    for r, ch in enumerate(s):
        while ch in window:     # the new character clashes: shrink from the left
            window.remove(s[l])
            l += 1
        window.add(ch)
        best = max(best, r - l + 1)
    return best

for s in ["abcbdeab", "bbbb", "pwwkew", ""]:
    print(repr(s), longest_unique(s))
```

The `while` inside the `for` looks quadratic, but `l` only ever moves right. Each index enters the window once and leaves it at most once:

$$
\text{adds} + \text{removals} \le n + n = 2n
$$

:::callout{kind=complexity time="O(n)" space="O(k)"}
Linear time; the set never holds more than k characters, where k is the size of the alphabet.
:::

## Windows that must contain something

For "the smallest window of `s` that contains every character of `t`", the roles flip: grow until the window is *valid* (it covers `t`), then shrink while it stays valid, recording the smallest. Counting how many characters are still missing keeps each check O(1):

```python run
from collections import Counter

def min_window(s, t):
    need = Counter(t)
    missing = len(t)
    best = (float("inf"), 0, 0)
    l = 0
    for r, ch in enumerate(s):
        if need[ch] > 0:
            missing -= 1
        need[ch] -= 1
        while missing == 0:              # valid: try to shrink it
            if r - l + 1 < best[0]:
                best = (r - l + 1, l, r + 1)
            need[s[l]] += 1
            if need[s[l]] > 0:
                missing += 1             # we just gave up a needed character
            l += 1
    return s[best[1]:best[2]] if best[0] != float("inf") else ""

print(min_window("ADOBECODEBANC", "ABC"))  # BANC
```

:::callout{kind=pitfall title="Shrink with while, not if"}
One new character can make several characters on the left removable at once. An `if` shrinks by a single step and leaves the window too wide.
:::

:::question{slug=longest-substring-without-repeating-characters}

:::question{slug=minimum-window-substring}

checkpoint.prompt_md: A window of size k slides one step to the right. How much work updates its sum?
checkpoint.explanation_md: Subtract the element that left and add the one that arrived: two operations, whatever k is.

checkpoint.explanation_md: Across the whole run there are at most n additions and n removals, so the total work is O(n).

choices: The highest price may come before the lowest
checkpoint.explanation_md: You must buy before you sell. The running minimum pairs each day only with earlier purchase days.

checkpoint.explanation_md: Each character enters the window once and leaves it at most once.

modules.title: Sorting & Recursion
modules.summary: How sorting works and when to lean on it; recursion and backtracking to explore every choice.

lessons.title: Sorting by insertion
lessons.body_md:
Insertion sort is how many people sort a hand of cards: take the next card and slide it left past every larger card until it fits. It is rarely the fastest choice, but its invariant — *the left part is always sorted* — is the model for reasoning about every sorting algorithm.

## Watch the sorted prefix grow

:::viz{id=insertion-sort}

```python run
def insertion_sort(a):
    shifts = 0
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        key = a[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and a[j] > key:   # shift larger elements one place right
            a[j + 1] = a[j]
            j -= 1
            shifts += 1
        a[j + 1] = key                 # drop the key into the gap
    return a, shifts

print(insertion_sort([5, 2, 8, 4, 7, 1, 6]))
print(insertion_sort([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]))  # sorted already: no shifts
print(insertion_sort([7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]))  # reversed: every pair shifts
```

Each shift repairs exactly one pair that was out of order (an *inversion*), so the work equals the number of inversions: none for sorted input, every pair for reversed input.

$$
0 \le \text{shifts} \le \frac{n(n-1)}{2}
$$

:::callout{kind=complexity time="O(n²) worst, O(n) nearly sorted" space="O(1)"}
In place, and fast on data that is almost sorted — which is why production sorts such as Timsort and introsort switch to insertion sort for short runs.
:::

:::callout{kind=note title="Stability"}
Insertion sort is **stable**: equal elements keep their original order, because a key never moves past an equal value (the test is `a[j] > key`, not `>=`). Stability matters when you sort records by one field and then by another.
:::

:::question{slug=meeting-rooms}

lessons.title: Sorting as a tool
lessons.body_md:
You will rarely write a sort by hand, and you will constantly *use* one. Sorting costs O(n log n) and buys structure: equal items become neighbours, overlapping ranges become adjacent, and the smallest and largest items move to the ends where two pointers can reach them.

## How fast can sorting be?

A comparison sort learns about the order only by comparing pairs, and each comparison has two outcomes. Telling all n! possible orders apart takes at least log₂(n!) comparisons, and

$$
\log_2 (n!) \approx n \log_2 n - 1.44\,n
$$

so no comparison sort beats O(n log n) in the worst case. Merge sort and heapsort reach that bound, and so does Timsort, the algorithm behind Python's `sorted`.

## Sort by a key

Sort records by one field with a key function, and by several fields with a tuple:

```python run
people = [("ada", 36), ("alan", 41), ("grace", 36), ("edsger", 72)]

print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1]))           # by age; ties keep input order
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0])))  # oldest first, then by name
```

:::callout{kind=pitfall title="JavaScript sorts numbers as strings"}
Without a comparator, `Array.prototype.sort` compares elements as strings, so `10` sorts before `9`:

```javascript run
console.log([10, 9, 1, 100].sort());                // [ 1, 10, 100, 9 ]
console.log([10, 9, 1, 100].sort((a, b) => a - b)); // [ 1, 9, 10, 100 ]
```
:::

## Merging intervals

Overlaps are hard to find among intervals in arbitrary order and trivial once they are sorted by start: an interval overlaps the merged block before it exactly when it starts before that block ends.

```python run
def merge(intervals):
    merged = []
    for start, end in sorted(intervals):          # by start time
        if merged and start <= merged[-1][1]:     # overlaps the last block
            merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], end)
        else:
            merged.append([start, end])
    return merged

print(merge([[8, 10], [1, 3], [2, 6], [15, 18], [17, 20]]))
# [[1, 6], [8, 10], [15, 20]]
```

"Can one person attend every meeting?" is the same scan asking a yes/no question: after sorting by start time, any meeting that starts before the previous one ends is a conflict.

:::callout{kind=complexity time="O(n log n)" space="O(n)"}
The sort dominates; the merge itself is one linear pass.
:::

:::question{slug=merge-intervals}

:::question{slug=three-sum}

lessons.title: Recursion and backtracking
lessons.body_md:
A recursive function solves a problem by solving a smaller copy of it. Two parts are non-negotiable: a **base case** that answers directly, and a **recursive case** that moves strictly toward it. Everything else — including backtracking, the technique behind subsets, permutations and puzzles — builds on those two.

## Every subset: include or exclude

Each element is either in a subset or not. Deciding element by element makes a binary tree of choices with one leaf per subset:

$$
\text{subsets of } n \text{ elements} = 2^n
$$

```python run
def subsets(nums):
    out, path = [], []

    def go(i):
        if i == len(nums):       # base case: every element decided
            out.append(path[:])  # record a *copy* of the current choices
            return
        go(i + 1)                # leave nums[i] out
        path.append(nums[i])     # choose it...
        go(i + 1)                # ...explore...
        path.pop()               # ...and un-choose it (backtrack)

    go(0)
    return out

print(subsets([1, 2, 3]))
print(len(subsets(list(range(10)))))  # 1024
```

## Choose, explore, un-choose

That last pattern is **backtracking**: make a choice, recurse, then undo the choice so the next branch starts clean. *Pruning* — refusing a choice that can never lead to a valid answer — is what makes it fast in practice. Generating balanced parentheses only adds a `)` when the prefix would stay balanced:

```python run
def parens(n):
    out = []

    def go(s, opened, closed):
        if len(s) == 2 * n:
            out.append(s)
            return
        if opened < n:
            go(s + "(", opened + 1, closed)
        if closed < opened:        # prune: never close more than we opened
            go(s + ")", opened, closed + 1)

    go("", 0, 0)
    return out

print(parens(3))
```

:::callout{kind=pitfall title="Record a copy"}
`out.append(path)` stores a reference to the single list that backtracking keeps changing, so every recorded subset ends up empty. Append `path[:]` (or `list(path)`).
:::

:::callout{kind=complexity time="O(n · 2ⁿ)" space="O(n)"}
2ⁿ subsets, each copied in O(n). The recursion is only n calls deep.
:::

:::question{slug=subsets}

:::question{slug=generate-parentheses}

Without a comparator the elements are compared as strings: "1" < "10" < "100" < "9". Pass `(a, b) => a - b`.

checkpoint.prompt_md: Why does the subset generator record `path[:]` rather than `path`?
choices: `path` keeps changing after it is recorded
checkpoint.explanation_md: Backtracking mutates one shared list. Without a copy, every recorded subset is the same list, which ends up empty.

checkpoint.prompt_md: How many subsets does a set of 5 elements have (including the empty set)?
checkpoint.explanation_md: Each of the 5 elements is independently in or out: 2⁵ = 32.
